<reason>Both sides were competent and stayed on the motion's ranking question, but Side A (CON) controlled the decisive clash. A's timing/positional-goods frame ("the advantage is bought during childhood, in real time; bequests arrive after the race is run"; "tax the bidding, not the funeral") gave the judge a concrete metric for comparing threats, and A repeatedly converted B's own mechanism against it: B admitted the head start is financed out of investment income by living parents, which A used to argue the funeral-timed instrument misses the causal channel. A's pressure questions were genuinely pointed and extracted a damaging admission ("the tax may collect nothing") plus an implicit slide toward periodic charges on live capital, which A crystallized as "that is my instrument under another name." A also supplied a specific, hard-to-tax channel (company-owned flat, fees paid direct to the school, guaranteed loans, family-firm salary) that B never fully absorbed. B answered honestly and in the required A1:/A2: format, defended design (aggregation of gifts, trust coverage, installments, high exemptions) plausibly, and landed one genuinely strong reframe — that A's preferred lever taxes dynastic capital income, not high earners' wages, so A's alternative arguably concedes the motion's comparison. That was B's best route to victory, but it appeared late and was asserted rather than developed into the centerpiece, and B's "ownership matters even if distributions are taxed" claim stayed closer to assertion than to a mechanism after A's "queue, not asset bases" reply. A's rebuttal-2 overrun/clip is a real execution cost, but the substance mostly landed before the cut. Net: a clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question 1 (name the pound the tax collects from the surgeon's daughter) forced B to concede "the tax may collect nothing," which A then used to argue that B's own case study of purchased childhood advantage lies outside B's chosen instrument. B's sharpest counterpunch — that A relabels dynastic returns as "annual income" while the motion's comparator is high earners' wages, not every capital tax — was the best available answer but arrived too late and under-weighted to neutralize the frame.</best_rebuttal>
